q: How many fleets participated in Run on Less – Messy Middle, and how were they split across powertrain types?
expected: 13 fleets total: 4 diesel/renewable diesel (Albert Transport, Frito-Lay, Mesilla Valley Transportation, Schneider), 3 CNG/RNG (Kleysen Group, UPS, Wegmans), 4 battery electric (4Gen Logistics, Joyride Logistics, Nevoya, Saia), and 2 hydrogen fuel cell (Penske, Pilot).

selected.why: It is the primary blueprint and overview report for Run on Less - Messy Middle, detailing the participating fleets and their powertrain splits.

answer:
A total of 13 fleets participated in the 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle demonstration [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20, 25]. The demonstration evaluated the real-world performance of Class 8 heavy-duty trucks (both sleepers and day cabs) operating in long-haul return-to-base and over-the-road duty cycles [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20]. 

The 13 participating fleets were split across four distinct powertrain categories as follows [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 25]:

*   **Diesel, Biodiesel, or Renewable Diesel (4 fleets):** Albert Transport (operating a 2022 Freightliner Cascadia on diesel), Frito-Lay (operating a Volvo VNL on B99 biodiesel), Mesilla Valley Transportation (operating an International LT on diesel), and Schneider (operating an International LT on renewable diesel) [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 29, 30, 31, 33, 34].
*   **Battery Electric Vehicles (4 fleets):** 4Gen Logistics (operating a 2024 Volvo VNR BEV), Joyride Logistics (operating a Windrose sleeper BEV), Nevoya (operating a Freightliner eCascadia day cab BEV), and Saia (operating two Tesla Semis) [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 29, 38, 39, 40].
*   **Natural Gas or Renewable Natural Gas (3 fleets):** Kleysen Group (operating a 2025 Kenworth T880), UPS (operating a Kenworth T680), and Wegmans (operating a Peterbilt 567) [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 29, 35, 36, 37].
*   **Hydrogen Fuel Cell (2 fleets):** Penske and Pilot, both operating Hyundai XCIENT fuel cell day cabs [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 29, 41, 42, 43].

q: How many drivers has NACFE engaged across all five Run on Less demonstrations to date, and how many interviews did NACFE conduct specifically for Messy Middle?
expected: 63 drivers across all five Run on Less demonstrations to date. For Messy Middle specifically, NACFE conducted 105 interviews across the 13 sites between June 3 and July 23, 2025 (48 of those interviews were with support-organization personnel rather than fleet staff).

selected.why: It directly states the total number of drivers engaged across all five Run on Less demonstrations to date and the specific number of interviews conducted for Messy Middle.

answer:
Across all five of its Run on Less demonstrations to date, the North American Council for Freight Efficiency (NACFE) has engaged a total of 63 drivers as they performed their usual commercial transport duties [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 49]. Specifically for the Run on Less – Messy Middle demonstration, NACFE conducted 105 interviews to gather real-world insights into alternative powertrain options [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 28, 49].

These 105 interviews were filmed during site visits conducted over a two-month period between June 3, 2025, and July 23, 2025, at the 13 participating fleet locations in the United States and Canada [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 28, 29, 64]. The interviewees represented a broad spectrum of the industry, including truck drivers, fleet managers, sustainability managers, operations managers, and executive leadership [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 49]. 

Additionally, 48 of the 105 interviews were conducted with key members of external support groups, such as vehicle manufacturers (OEMs), utility representatives, charging equipment suppliers, project funders, and truck dealers [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 28, 50]. These interviews contributed to more than 30 production videos released by NACFE to help bring clarity to the operational realities of Class 8 decarbonization [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 49, 68].

q: According to the NREL source cited in this report, what share of the trucking market does the long-haul segment represent, and what share of emissions does it contribute?
expected: Long-haul trucking is 9% of the trucking market but contributes 48% of the industry's emissions, per NREL's "Decarbonizing Medium- & Heavy-Duty On-Road Vehicles: Zero-Emission Vehicle Cost Analysis" (2022), as cited by NACFE.

selected.why: This report explicitly cites NREL's 'Decarbonizing Medium- & Heavy-Duty On-Road Vehicles' report regarding the long-haul segment's market share and emissions contribution.

answer:
According to the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) report cited by NACFE, the Class 8 long-haul segment represents **9% of the trucking market** but contributes **48% of its emissions** [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20, 62].

These figures come from NREL’s report, *Decarbonizing Medium- & Heavy-Duty On-Road Vehicles: Zero Emission Vehicles Cost Analysis* [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20]. 

This disproportionate emissions footprint is the primary reason NACFE focused its 2025 *Run on Less – Messy Middle* demonstration on the Class 8 long-haul segment [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20]. Because this segment generates nearly half of the industry's emissions, understanding and implementing the best alternative powertrain solutions for these duty cycles is considered critical to decarbonizing the trucking industry as a whole [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20, 22].

q: According to the "What is 0.5 MPG worth?" infographic (Figure 32), what elevation gain, temperature deviation, and cargo weight increase are each shown as roughly equivalent to a 0.5 MPG fuel-economy impact, and how much does 10-15 MPH of extra speed above optimal cost in MPG?
expected: 250 feet of elevation gain, a 10°F deviation above or below 80°F, and a 10,000 lb weight increase are each shown as contributing factors. Traveling 10 MPH above optimal speed costs about 1 MPG, and 15 MPH above optimal costs about 2 MPG.

selected.source_matched_by: matches the mention of a 10,000 lb weight difference affecting fuel economy by approximately 0.5 MPG from prior Run on Less findings referenced in the blueprint report.
selected.why: The blueprint report references NACFE's prior Run on Less findings regarding weight, speed, and fuel-economy equivalents.

answer:
According to the "What is 0.5 MPG worth?" infographic (Figure 32), the conditions shown as roughly equivalent to a 0.5 MPG fuel-economy impact are:
* **Elevation gain:** 250 ft. [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 56]
* **Temperature deviation:** 10° F above or below the baseline of 80° F [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 56]
* **Cargo/vehicle weight increase:** 10,000 lbs. [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 56]

Additionally, driving at speeds above the optimal limit incurs a higher fuel economy penalty. Running at 10 mph above the optimal speed costs 1 MPG in fuel efficiency, while running at 15 mph above the optimal speed costs 2 MPG [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 56]. For comparison, driving just 7 mph above the optimal speed is shown as equivalent to the 0.5 MPG penalty [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 56].

q: According to NACFE's dedicated TCO report, what does it conclude about the total cost of ownership comparison across the four Messy Middle powertrains?
expected: BEVs are projected to achieve the lowest net TCO of any powertrain in every one of the five modeled duty cycles by 2035, driven by falling battery/vehicle prices, while diesel faces a 'cost escalator' (rising maintenance, insurance, and emissions-compliance costs) that erodes its current advantage even as fuel cost per mile drops slightly. Per-duty-cycle 2035 figures include: Long-Haul OTR, diesel's current $0.61/mile advantage flips, with BEVs undercutting diesel by $0.09/mile; Regional Linehaul, BEV $0.94/mile vs. diesel $1.00/mile; Regional RTB, BEV $1.13/mile vs. diesel $1.29/mile (a 12% BEV advantage); Urban/Metro P&D, BEV $1.92/mile vs. diesel $2.43/mile; Drayage/Port Shuttles, BEV about $0.19/mile cheaper than diesel. CNG/RNG serves as a stable near-term hedge but is eventually overtaken by BEVs in most duty cycles; FCEV remains the most expensive option through 2035, tethered to hydrogen delivery price ($4-$15/kg modeled). The analysis assumes no incentives, as a conservative baseline.
expected_loc: TCO report, Section 1.4-1.5 (Key Findings by Powertrain / by Duty Cycle)

selected.why: This report is NACFE's dedicated TCO companion report for the Messy Middle and explicitly provides the total cost of ownership projections and comparisons across all four powertrains and five duty cycles.

answer:
According to NACFE’s dedicated total cost of ownership (TCO) report, there is no universal date for cost parity; instead, TCO is highly bespoke and represents an operational window defined by a fleet's specific geography, duty cycle, and asset utilization [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 18, 20, 101]. Despite this localized variability, the report’s baseline modeling concludes that battery electric vehicles (BEVs) are the definitive long-term economic winners, achieving the lowest net TCO across all five studied duty cycles by 2035 [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 18, 21, 101]. This transition is driven by a projected 45% drop in BEV purchase prices, superior energy efficiency, stable electricity costs, and a maturing secondary market for zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) assets [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 81, 101].

Conversely, the era of legacy diesel as the undisputed low-cost leader is ending [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 101]. A "diesel cost escalator" driven by emissions compliance, fuel price volatility, and rising maintenance and insurance costs is steadily raising its net TCO over time [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 81, 101]. In the near term (2025 and 2028), compressed natural gas and renewable natural gas (CNG/RNG) serve as a stable, infrastructure-ready financial hedge that frequently undercuts diesel [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 21, 81, 101]. However, because CNG/RNG costs remain relatively flat, they are eventually overtaken by BEVs by 2035 [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 21, 81]. Hydrogen fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs) remain the most expensive option in almost all scenarios, but they find a clear niche in high-utilization, heavy-haul OTR lanes where payload capacity and rapid fueling are non-negotiable [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 21, 81, 101].

These conclusions are supported by per-mile TCO figures calculated under specific operating conditions, assuming 268 operating days per year [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 63]:

*   **Regional Return-to-Base (RTB):** Under conditions of 244 average daily miles (65,481 annual miles), this represents the "Goldilocks" scenario for electrification [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 22, 63]. In 2025, diesel leads at a net TCO of $1.07 per mile, while BEVs cost $1.86 per mile [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 109]. By 2035, BEVs drop to $1.13 per mile, decisively beating diesel, which climbs to $1.29 per mile [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 109].
*   **Long-Haul Over-the-Road (OTR):** Under high-utilization conditions of 555 average daily miles (148,740 annual miles) [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 63], diesel remains the cost leader in 2025 at $0.85 per mile, compared to BEVs at $1.46 per mile and FCEVs at $1.71 per mile [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 108]. By 2035, BEVs achieve parity and narrowly win the segment at $0.90 per mile, undercutting diesel ($0.99 per mile) and CNG/RNG ($0.98 per mile), while FCEVs narrow their gap to $1.09 per mile [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 108].
*   **Urban Package & Delivery (P&D):** Under low-utilization conditions of 80 average daily miles (21,440 annual miles) [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 63], ZEVs are heavily penalized in 2025, with BEVs costing $4.29 per mile compared to diesel's $1.83 per mile [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 109]. By 2035, falling vehicle prices allow BEVs to undercut diesel organically at $1.92 per mile versus diesel's $2.43 per mile [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 109].

q: What has NACFE found about total cost of ownership for last-mile electric delivery vans?
expected: NACFE's 2024 Electric DEPOT report found last-mile electric vans/step vans already have upfront costs much closer to parity with gas/diesel than heavier Class 8 vehicles, and classifies them as 'small energy depots' (under 10 MWh/day) that are 'ready to electrify now' because long overnight dwell times allow slow, low-cost managed charging that avoids demand charges. Real examples tracked: Frito-Lay's Ford E-Transit vans (68-kWh battery, ~108-mile range) in Queens, NY, and Purolator's Motiv EPIC step vans (127-kWh battery, ~105-mile range, 4-60 mile daily routes) in Richmond, BC. NACFE cautions that standard TCO spreadsheets often miss uptime gains, the fleet's operational learning curve, and regional incentives like California's LCFS credits. Note this is a narrower/different scope than the 2026 TCO report, which models Class 8 vehicles only and does not cover vans.
expected_loc: p.34 (Frito-Lay E-Transit), p.43 (Purolator Motiv EPIC), p.77-79 (small energy depot framing, Figure 57)

selected.why: Covers Class 3-5 electric vans and step vans (like BrightDrop and E-Transit) and depot electrification dynamics explored during Run on Less - Electric DEPOT.
Provides detailed TCO projections across duty cycles including Urban/Metro Pickup & Delivery (last-mile delivery) for electric vehicles over timeframes up to 2035.

answer:
NACFE has found that last-mile electric delivery vans and step vans have upfront capital costs that are much closer to parity with gasoline and diesel vehicles than any other medium- or heavy-duty electric vehicle (EV) segment [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, p. 79]. Consequently, they represent low total cost of ownership (TCO) opportunities and are ready for widespread fleet deployment immediately [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, p. 79]. When operated out of "small energy depots" requiring less than 10 MWh of power per day, these fleets can leverage long, slow, and relatively inexpensive overnight Level 2 charging to drastically minimize electricity and charging infrastructure costs [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, p. 43, 78-79]. 

Despite these positive economic indicators, NACFE noted in its 2024 *Electric Depot* report that calculating a precise, standardized TCO for electric vans remains a challenge for fleets [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, p. 77]. Traditional TCO calculations often fail to capture qualitative variables such as improved vehicle uptime, the learning curve of transitioning a fleet, or the financial benefits of regional incentives like California's Low Carbon Fuel Standard (LCFS) credits [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, p. 77] [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 30]. (Note that NACFE’s subsequent 2026 TCO report focused exclusively on Class 8 heavy-duty vehicles and omitted light- and medium-duty delivery vans [run-on-less-messy-middle-tco-2026, p. 19]).

Real-world operational data from depots operating last-mile delivery fleets—such as Frito-Lay in New York and Purolator in British Columbia—supports this low-TCO business case due to the duty cycles of these vehicles [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, p. 33, 42]. For instance, Ford E-Transit vans (equipped with a 68-kWh battery and an estimated range of 108 miles) and Motiv EPIC step vans (featuring a 127-kWh battery and an estimated 105-mile range) operate on short, dense urban routes with multiple stops and diminishing loads [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, p. 34, 43]. At Purolator's Richmond depot, where daily van routes range from 4 to 60 miles per day, Level 2 overhead chargers were sufficient to fully recharge the vehicles overnight [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, p. 43]. This lower daily mileage and predictable return-to-base routing dramatically reduce the need for high-power, expensive utility upgrades or public charging [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, p. 34].

q: How many Run on Less demonstrations has NACFE conducted to date?
expected: Five, as of the Run on Less – Messy Middle report (published January 2026): 2017 (diesel long-haul), 2019 Regional, 2021 Electric, 2023 Electric DEPOT, and 2025 Messy Middle. A naive answer sourced from the older Run on Less – Electric DEPOT report (published May 2024) would say four, since it predates the Messy Middle Run and states 'NACFE has conducted four Run on Less demonstrations so far.' The current, correct count is five.

selected.why: The abstract explicitly states this is the overview report for Run on Less - Messy Middle, 'NACFE's fifth Run on Less demonstration,' and discusses findings across 'all five Run on Less demonstrations to date.'

answer:
NACFE has conducted five Run on Less demonstrations to date [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20]. These biennial demonstrations are designed to highlight commercially available, real-world technologies that can help fleets improve freight efficiency and reduce emissions [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20, 22]. 

As detailed in the provided report, the five demonstrations are:

*   **2017 Run on Less (Long Haul):** This initial event highlighted Class 8 diesel tractors in real-world, long-haul fleet operations. The 7 participating fleets achieved an average fuel economy of 10.1 MPG over the course of the three-week demonstration [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20, 62].
*   **2019 Run on Less Regional:** This event focused on Class 8 tractors in real-world regional haul operations [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20]. The sources contain a minor discrepancy regarding the average fuel economy measured during this three-week regional duty cycle, noting 8.3 MPG in one section [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20] and 8.4 MPG in another [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 62]. 
*   **2021 Run on Less – Electric:** This event illustrated fleet transition to battery electric vehicles (BEVs). It featured 13 fleets piloting terminal tractors, vans, step vans, medium-duty box trucks, and heavy-duty regional haul tractors [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20].
*   **2023 Run on Less – Electric DEPOT:** This demonstration focused on fleet scaling and infrastructure, highlighting 10 depots that each operated 15 or more Class 3 to 8 BEVs [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20, 62].
*   **2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle:** The most recent demonstration followed 13 fleets operating Class 8 sleepers and day cabs in long-haul return-to-base and over-the-road duty cycles [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20]. It evaluated four distinct powertrain solutions: diesel/renewable diesel, natural gas/renewable natural gas, battery electric, and hydrogen fuel cells [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20].

q: In total, how many drivers has NACFE engaged across all of its Run on Less demonstrations?
expected: 63 drivers, per the Run on Less – Messy Middle report (published January 2026), which covers all five demonstrations to date. A naive answer sourced from the older Run on Less – Electric DEPOT report (published May 2024) would say 48 drivers, since that report only covers the first four demonstrations ('During the four Run on Less demonstrations, NACFE engaged with 48 drivers'). The current, correct total is 63.

selected.why: Reports the cumulative driver count across prior Run on Less demonstrations up to that point.
Reports the cumulative driver count across all five Run on Less demonstrations including Messy Middle.

answer:
NACFE has engaged a total of 63 drivers across all five of its Run on Less demonstrations [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 49]. These drivers have participated in real-world freight operations while having their shifts, routes, and performance tracked to help evaluate the effectiveness of various vehicle efficiency and powertrain technologies [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 49, 50; Electric Truck Depots Are Evolving: How 10 Fleets Grew Their BEV Populations, p. 64]. 

The cumulative driver count has grown alongside the expanding scope of the biennial demonstrations. Up through the fourth event—the 2023 *Run on Less – Electric DEPOT* demonstration—NACFE had engaged with 48 drivers across four events, with that specific 2023 run utilizing a then-record 18 participating drivers [Electric Truck Depots Are Evolving: How 10 Fleets Grew Their BEV Populations, p. 64]. The fifth demonstration, the 2025 *Run on Less – Messy Middle*, which tracked 13 fleets operating a variety of powertrain solutions, added more participants to bring the historical total to the current 63 drivers [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20, 49].

These participating operators represent a diverse group with a wide range of backgrounds, ethnicities, ages, genders, and experience levels—including some with over 40 years of driving experience [Electric Truck Depots Are Evolving: How 10 Fleets Grew Their BEV Populations, p. 65; How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 49]. Their firsthand insights, recorded during on-site interviews, are combined with continuous telematics tracking data to help the trucking industry better understand the operational benefits, driver comfort, and technical challenges of advanced diesel, natural gas, battery electric, and hydrogen fuel cell powertrains [Electric Truck Depots Are Evolving: How 10 Fleets Grew Their BEV Populations, p. 65-66; How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 50].

q: What is the longest range demonstrated by a battery-electric Class 8 truck in NACFE's Run on Less research?
expected: The longest-range BEV NACFE has actually tracked is a PepsiCo Tesla Semi during the 2023 Run on Less – Electric DEPOT (report published May 2024): 'Tesla Semis saw ranges of 410 miles on a single charge and completed 1,076 miles in a 24-hour period' (p.39-40). The Run on Less – Messy Middle report (published January 2026) shows the 400+ mile BEV class has since become normal-fleet-operation reality rather than a single flagship vehicle, citing Joyride Logistics' Windrose sleeper tractor (705-kWh LFP pack) at up to 420 miles — while most other OEMs' production BEVs still run 150-250 miles per charge. A naive answer drawing only on the 2024 report's non-Tesla depot fleets (e.g. the OK Produce/Penske Freightliner eCascadia at 475-kWh/230 miles) would understate the 2023/2024 baseline by missing the PepsiCo Tesla Semi figure entirely.

selected.why: Covers BEV vehicle models, battery capacities, and ranges tracked during Run on Less - Electric DEPOT.
Reports on battery-electric Class 8 sleeper tractors and ranges observed during Run on Less - Messy Middle.

answer:
The longest single-charge range demonstrated by a battery-electric Class 8 truck in NACFE’s Run on Less research is **441 miles** (also reported as **410 miles** in some sections of the report) [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, pp. 40, 80]. Additionally, a Class 8 truck demonstrated a total daily operating range of **1,076 miles within a 24-hour period** by utilizing multiple fast-charging sessions [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, pp. 28, 40, 80]. 

The single-charge range of 441 miles (or 410 miles) was achieved during the 2023 *Run on Less – Electric DEPOT* by PepsiCo's fleet of Class 8 Tesla Semis operating out of Sacramento, California [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, pp. 39, 40, 80]. These heavy-duty trucks carried gross vehicle weight loads of up to 82,000 lbs. [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, p. 39]. To achieve the 1,076-mile distance in a 24-hour period, the PepsiCo Tesla Semi was "slip-seated," meaning it was driven by two drivers on separate shifts to keep the vehicle active nearly all day [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, pp. 39, 40]. The operation relied on ultra-fast 750 kW chargers, which allowed the truck to charge from a 10% to 95% state of charge in less than 30 minutes [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, p. 40]. 

Later research from the 2025 *Run on Less – Messy Middle* highlights additional battery-electric Class 8 capabilities. During this event, Joyride Logistics operated a Windrose battery-electric sleeper tractor with a 705-kWh LFP battery pack that is capable of traveling "up to 420 miles" [run-on-less-messy-middle-blueprint-2025, p. 39]. Additionally, Saia LTL Freight introduced Tesla Semis to its fleet with a "claimed 500-mile range" under typical less-than-truckload (LTL) conditions, though this was noted as a claimed specification rather than a measured performance figure from the Run [run-on-less-messy-middle-blueprint-2025, p. 41].

q: In 2023, NACFE described typical production battery-electric truck range as 150-250 miles per charge (with Tesla's unverified 500-mile demo as an outlier achieved under near-ideal conditions and a low, 55-mph speed limit). How does that compare with what NACFE actually measured in real fleet operation during the 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle?
expected: The 2023 white paper 'The Messy Middle: A Time for Action' reported that production BEVs from Daimler, Volvo, Kenworth, Peterbilt and others offered single-charge ranges of 150-250 miles, cautioning that Tesla's December 2022 500-mile demonstration used nearly 100% of battery state of charge (versus the recommended 20-80% range) and was run at California's 55 mph truck speed limit — not representative of typical operations. In the actual 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle, run in real revenue service (not a controlled demo), NACFE tracked a Windrose battery-electric sleeper (Joyride Logistics) with a real-world quoted range of up to 420 miles, and its Initial Findings list '400+ mile battery electric vehicles' among recent powertrain advancements — roughly double the typical 2023 production range, achieved in normal fleet duty cycles rather than a one-off demonstration.
expected_loc: p.26/p.30-31 (2023 baseline); current: run-on-less-messy-middle-blueprint-2025, p.39, p.66-67

selected.why: Establishes NACFE's 2023 baseline stating production heavy-duty BEVs had a typical 150-250 mile single-charge range.
Contains the actual operational and telematics data measured for Class 8 BEVs during the September 2025 Run on Less - Messy Middle demonstration.

answer:
Real-world measurements taken during the September 2025 *Run on Less – Messy Middle* demonstration reveal a significant step-change in battery-electric vehicle (BEV) capabilities compared to NACFE's 2023 baseline expectations. In 2023, NACFE cited typical production BEV single-charge ranges as 150 to 250 miles [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 30]. While mid-capacity regional trucks in the 2025 Run still operated within this practical range, larger battery capacities (700 to 900+ kWh) combined with strategic corridor fast charging enabled trucks to achieve daily distances between 350 and 875 miles, proving that 500-plus mile days are no longer unverified outliers [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 159, 204].

For regional, return-to-base operations, the 2025 measurements closely matched NACFE's earlier baseline expectations. Nevoya’s Freightliner eCascadia (438 kWh usable battery) achieved a daily average of 173 miles and a maximum single-day distance of 348 miles under regional distribution conditions in California's Central Valley, maintaining a payload-dependent single-charge Probable Maximum Range (PMR) of 150 to 200 miles with payloads averaging 63,000 lbs on terrain with approximately 90% of miles under a 3% grade [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 180, 181]. Similarly, 4Gen's Volvo VNR Electric (565 kWh battery) logged an average of 201 miles per day and peaked at 388 miles under Southern California drayage conditions (~80% of miles under 3% grade), demonstrating a practical single-charge PMR of 180 to 220 miles [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 161-162].

In contrast, long-haul BEV deployments shattered the 250-mile ceiling. Saia’s second Tesla Semi (500-mile configuration, estimated 800 to 900 kWh battery) averaged 372 miles per day and achieved a validated single-day maximum of 660 miles under LTL long-haul terminal-to-terminal conditions (~81% of miles under 3% grade), with an observed single-charge PMR of 350 to 450 miles [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 197-198]. Furthermore, JoyRide's Windrose sleeper (705 kWh LFP battery) averaged 409 miles per day and achieved a validated maximum daily distance of 875 miles while hauling payloads ranging from 39,700 to 81,600 lbs across Western US highway corridors (~96% of miles under 3% grade), demonstrating a single-charge PMR of 350 to 400 miles [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 170-171, 175-176]. 

These extended operations did not rely on unrepresentative 55-mph speed trials. Instead, they succeeded through high-power DC fast charging strategically integrated into natural operational dwell times and driver breaks [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 159, 206]. However, NACFE notes that these high-productivity milestones still depend heavily on favorable terrain and well-sited corridor charging, as steep grades (6% or greater) continue to impose severe energy consumption penalties that reduce BEV efficiency by up to half [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 206-207].

q: NACFE's 2023 white paper laid out a suggested sequence for fleets choosing a powertrain (start with BEV, then hydrogen fuel cell, then natural gas/hybrids/renewable fuels, then efficient diesel as a fallback), while also acknowledging this was 'an oversimplification.' Did the real-world results of the 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle, which tested all four options side by side, support a single best powertrain choice or confirm the need for fleet-specific evaluation?
expected: The 2023 white paper's 'Framework for Powertrain Decision Making' (Figure 15) suggests fleets start with BEV, fall back to hydrogen fuel cell, then natural gas/hybrids/renewable fuels, and finally efficient diesel, while explicitly noting fleets will likely need multiple, duty-cycle-specific decisions rather than one universal answer. NACFE reused this same framework graphic in the 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle report, and that Run's real-world findings confirmed the 2023 premise rather than crowning one winner: 'the real-world results are that all four technologies are performing well in this segment of the market and there is no one right choice for all fleets. Rather powertrain choice depends on the intricacies of each fleet's operation, the length of haul, access to fueling/charging and a host of other factors.'
expected_loc: p.9, p.38 (2023 framework); current: run-on-less-messy-middle-blueprint-2025, p.24 (Figure 3, reused framework), p.62-63 (findings)

selected.why: The Run on Less - Messy Middle blueprint report covers the 2025 demonstration of all four powertrains side-by-side and directly addresses whether the results support a single best powertrain or fleet-specific evaluation.

This deep operational companion report provides the comprehensive cross-fleet telematics and analysis from the September 2025 Run on Less - Messy Middle, evaluating how different powertrains perform across various duty cycles.

answer:
The real-world results of the 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle demonstration did not support a single best powertrain choice. Instead, they confirmed the critical need for fleet-specific and route-specific evaluation [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 62; Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 232]. NACFE concluded that no single technology is capable of addressing every freight application with optimal economics, environmental performance, and operational simplicity [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 228]. 

Instead, the demonstration showed that all four tested technologies—diesel, natural gas, battery electric, and hydrogen fuel cell—perform well, but each has a specific operational envelope where it excels, as well as clear physical or infrastructural boundaries where it struggles [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 62; Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 28]. For example:
* **Diesel and Renewable Diesel:** These fleets served as the ultimate benchmark for flexibility and range. Highly optimized diesel setups achieved between 9.0 and 11.8 MPG [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 29]. This performance represents nearly double the typical industry fleet average of approximately 6.0 MPG [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 78]. Renewable diesel offered a drop-in 50% to 80% carbon intensity reduction with zero operational changes [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 252, 254].
* **Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs):** BEVs proved commercially viable for regional and selected long-haul corridors, achieving 1.5 to 2.0 kWh/mi (overall ranges between 0.44 to 6.71 mi/kWh depending on conditions) [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 29, 205]. The largest battery packs (705 kWh) achieved impressive daily averages of approximately 409 miles per active day and a maximum single-day distance of 875 miles under favorable conditions [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 170]. However, BEVs showed extreme terrain sensitivity, with efficiency dropping by 50% to 70% on grades greater than 3%, meaning route-specific terrain profiling is absolutely necessary [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 206, 252]. 
* **CNG/RNG:** Utilizing the 15-liter Cummins X15N engine, natural gas trucks delivered 4.5 to 6.7 mi/DGE [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 29]. They successfully handled very heavy-haul assignments, such as regional fuel tankers and triple dry-van configurations weighing 100,000 to 140,000 lbs. gross combination weight (GCW) [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 121, 147]. However, CNG efficiency severely degraded in low-speed, stop-and-go urban environments, establishing their ideal envelope as highway-dominant cruising with predictable station access [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 122, 254].
* **Hydrogen Fuel Cells (FCEVs):** FCEVs demonstrated rapid 10-to-15-minute refueling and a highly usable range of 350 to 450 miles on 68.6 kg of usable hydrogen [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 211, 212, 253]. Unfortunately, they remain severely restricted by high fuel costs ($15 to $25/kg) and extreme infrastructure scarcity (with only approximately 60 heavy-duty stations nationwide) [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 253, 255].

Ultimately, the 2025 demonstration proved that forcing a powertrain mismatch creates operational friction and suboptimal economics [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 68]. Because route terrain, daily mileage, payload limits, and local infrastructure vary so widely, fleets cannot rely on generic manufacturer specification sheets or a single fallback option [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 234, 253]. Instead, navigating the "Messy Middle" transition requires "portfolio thinking," where fleets actively manage mixed-technology fleets and conduct rigorous, route-specific validations to match each vehicle to its optimal application [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 232, 233].

q: How many Guidance Reports had NACFE published on electric/hydrogen trucks as of early 2019, and how many had it published by mid-2025?
expected: As of early 2019, NACFE had produced three Guidance Reports: Electric Trucks: Where They Make Sense (May 2018), Medium-Duty Electric Trucks – Cost of Ownership (October 2018), and Amping Up – Charging Infrastructure for Electric Trucks (March 2019). By mid-2025, per the Run on Less – Messy Middle report, that had grown to 11 Guidance Reports on electric and hydrogen fuel cell trucks — nearly a fourfold increase over roughly six years.
expected_loc: p.10-11 (2019: three reports); current: run-on-less-messy-middle-blueprint-2025, p.20 (mid-2025: 11 reports)

It provides context on the later time point (mid-2025) through its description of the Messy Middle Bootcamp series and demonstration planning leading up to 2025/2026.

answer:
As of early 2019, the North American Council for Freight Efficiency (NACFE) had published **3** Guidance Reports focusing on electric trucks [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 11]. By mid-2025, NACFE had expanded this library to a total of **11** Guidance Reports covering electric and hydrogen fuel cell trucks [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 21].

The initial three reports, launched between May 2018 and March 2019, were designed to help guide the industry through early transformational changes. They focused on where electric trucks made sense, the total cost of ownership for medium-duty electric trucks, and the charging infrastructure required to support them [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 11]. 

As the transition toward zero-emission freight movement progressed, NACFE significantly expanded its research. By mid-2025, the 11 Guidance Reports provided fleets and manufacturers with unbiased, detailed reviews of emerging battery electric and hydrogen fuel cell technologies to assist them in navigating the complex decisions of the "messy middle" [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 21].

q: As of December 2022, how many public hydrogen fueling stations did the DOE report in North America, and how many of those were heavy-duty truck sites?

answer:
As of December 2022, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) reported only 60 public hydrogen fueling stations in North America for all vehicle types [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 24]. Out of those 60 stations, only 4 were heavy-duty truck hydrogen fueling sites [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 24]. 

The vast majority of these public stations were highly regionalized, with 53 of the 60 stations located in California [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 24]. Because the source report was published in 2023, these figures from late 2022 may not fully reflect the current state of hydrogen refueling infrastructure.

q: According to the 2023 messy middle white paper, what is the estimated overall energy efficiency (charger/tank to wheels) of battery electric trucks compared to internal combustion engine and hydrogen fuel cell trucks?
expected: BEVs: about 65% to 85% efficient from charger to wheels. ICE vehicles: approximately 40% to 50% efficient. Hydrogen fuel cell vehicles: approximately 30% to 50% efficient.

selected.why: The 2023 messy middle white paper explicitly details the overall energy efficiency of battery electric, internal combustion engine, and hydrogen fuel cell trucks in its key findings.

answer:
Battery electric vehicles (BEVs) offer the highest overall energy efficiency among commercial powertrain options, achieving an estimated efficiency of **65% to 85%** measured from the charger to the wheels [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 26]. 

By comparison, the overall energy efficiency of other powertrain options measured under similar tank/fuel-to-wheels conditions is significantly lower:
* **Internal Combustion Engine (ICE):** Approximately **40% to 50%** efficiency [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 26].
* **Hydrogen Fuel Cell (H2FC):** Approximately **30% to 50%** efficiency [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 26].

Because battery electric trucks lose far less energy during operation than ICE or hydrogen fuel cell systems, NACFE notes that BEVs represent the most energy-efficient powertrain solution currently available for goods movement [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 26].

answer:
During NACFE's Messy Middle Bootcamp Session 2 ("Decarbonizing with Natural Gas"), Marty Tufty, Corporate Fleet Manager for WM, reported that the company operates a fleet of over 13,000 Class 8 heavy-duty natural gas vehicles [Messy Middle Bootcamp Session 2 - Decarbonizing with Natural Gas, 38:50]. Within this fleet, more than 6,000 trucks run at NOx emissions levels below the 2027 standard (at 20 milligrams), a capability WM has maintained in its fleet since 2018 [Messy Middle Bootcamp Session 2 - Decarbonizing with Natural Gas, 38:50, 40:38]. 

WM’s fueling and facility infrastructure includes 213 designed, built, owned, operated, and maintained natural gas fueling stations, 25 of which are open to the public [Messy Middle Bootcamp Session 2 - Decarbonizing with Natural Gas, 38:50]. The fleet uses overhead truss slow-fill systems at its locations and manages over 200 maintenance facilities outfitted with custom-designed, live-monitored natural gas safety sensor systems [Messy Middle Bootcamp Session 2 - Decarbonizing with Natural Gas, 43:12, 43:43]. On the fuel supply side, WM's renewable energy division currently operates seven renewable natural gas (RNG) production facilities producing about 40 million diesel gallon equivalents (DGE) per year, with 17 additional facilities under construction to scale RNG output past 200 million DGE annually by 2026 [Messy Middle Bootcamp Session 2 - Decarbonizing with Natural Gas, 39:52].

To maintain and operate this equipment safely, WM has trained a dedicated workforce of over 2,000 technicians and over 10,000 drivers [Messy Middle Bootcamp Session 2 - Decarbonizing with Natural Gas, 38:50]. In total, WM has invested over $4 billion into its natural gas program, displacing 110 million gallons of diesel fuel in 2024 alone [Messy Middle Bootcamp Session 2 - Decarbonizing with Natural Gas, 38:50].
